title: Five votes for Sweden’s November hike concealed different views of the next one
summary: All five Riksbank board members supported raising the policy rate from 1.75% to 2% on 3 November. The minutes released on 10 November reveal a less uniform view of the next move. Per Jansson explicitly kept a December increase in play. Aino Bunge wanted to evaluate each step as changes in interest costs reached households. Göran Hjelm described circumstances in which he would have preferred to wait even with the same central inflation and activity forecasts. The common vote established the direction of travel. The individual statements reveal how differently the members might respond to the next inflation or employment surprise (minutes, pp. 6–22).

Market participants already expected the increase. Staff reported that analyst forecasts and market pricing both pointed to 2% ahead of the meeting. The spread between euro-area and Swedish yields had narrowed in October, helping the krona recover, even though it remained the weakest G10 currency against the dollar over the year to date. European gas prices had tripled during the year, and disruption to refining as well as oil shipments had driven the spread between crude and refined products to historically high levels. At the same time, flight to safety had brought some government yields down from their early-October highs. France was an exception as investors demanded compensation for fiscal and political risk. These developments were inputs into the meeting. They cannot be attributed to a Swedish decision that had not yet been announced (staff financial-market assessment, pp. 3–4).

Jansson’s distinction between headline and underlying inflation was quantitative. September CPIF inflation had risen to 1.5% from 0.7% in August, while its energy contribution rose from 0.3 percentage points to a full point. CPIF excluding energy held at 0.5%. Removing temporary fiscal effects put September inflation at 3.0% with energy and 1.6% without. Energy futures implied a decline, but those curves had systematically underestimated actual energy prices during the year. He worried that persistent cost increases, stronger demand and currency weakness could shift firms from occasional to routine pass-through. He invoked the 1970s and 1980s to explain the danger of a regime in which repeated cost increases become embedded in prices. He did not suggest Sweden was already in such a spiral (pp. 6–9).

The exchange-rate window also changed the interpretation. Since shortly after the September decision the krona had appreciated almost 3% against the euro and about 1% against the dollar. Jansson judged its earlier depreciation since the outbreak of war on 28 February still large enough to raise future inflation. Supporting the September path meant, in his reading, broadly preserving the cumulative amount of tightening, described as just under two additional increases. It did not commit the Board to exact meeting dates. The possibility of successive November and December moves therefore remained open in his individual assessment (p. 9).

Hjelm supplied the strongest evidence of upstream pressure. The import price index rose about 4.5% in September alone and almost 15% from the outbreak of the war, compared with roughly 40% between the summers of 2021 and 2022. Producer prices of inputs for the domestic market, excluding direct energy effects, had risen close to 10% since the war began. Yet indirect effects on consumer prices were still limited. The average historical correlation between producer and consumer prices had been weak. His concern was that a large shock combined with higher resource utilisation could increase pass-through disproportionately. Without the cost shock and its associated risk distribution, he said he would have waited for clearer evidence that spare labour capacity was being used, even given the same forecasts for resource utilisation and inflation (pp. 10–13).

Anna Seim stressed the distributional stakes. Rate increases quickly affect borrowers in an interest-sensitive economy, but inflation cuts purchasing power across the population. Households spending larger shares on necessities are especially exposed. She supported early action to reduce the likelihood of stronger tightening later, while acknowledging that fiscal support had temporarily lifted real incomes and that household confidence had weakened sharply in October. Bunge emphasised a related feedback. Higher rates, energy costs and the withdrawal of fiscal support could slow spending, reducing firms’ ability to pass on cost increases. Conversely, a broad change in pricing behaviour in a strong economy would warrant faster tightening. Both voted to raise rates. Their arguments put different weight on protecting real incomes and on the risk that cumulative borrowing costs could interrupt the recovery (pp. 13–18).

Governor Erik Thedéen described the September rate projection as a weighting of different possible outcomes. On the central outlook he still expected gradual increases over roughly the next six months. Stronger activity and cost pressure spreading across industries could warrant several more rises. Weaker demand or firms adapting to higher costs without passing them on could produce a shallower path. The data he cited included a forecast of nearly 3% GDP growth in 2026 and September retail durable goods sales almost 6% above a year earlier. At the same time, underlying inflation excluding energy and temporary fiscal effects had come in at 1.6%, below the 1.8% forecast, partly because travel prices rose less than expected. That miss mattered less to him than the broadening recovery and the risk of future cost pass-through (pp. 18–21).

The staff’s financial-stability assessment provides another channel relevant to those scenarios. Domestic credit was growing broadly in line with the real economy. Easier mortgage rules had increased the share of households borrowing more relative to home values, while aggregate debt grew alongside incomes. Commercial real estate still had high vacancies despite favourable funding conditions. Globally, leveraged non-banks could amplify a fiscal shock, and increasingly debt-financed AI investment created exposures that were difficult to trace. This evidence explains why financial risks could affect Sweden without a contemporaneous surge in domestic borrowing. It also sets a limit on what the minutes establish about policy effects: the record supplies pre-meeting prices and five members’ assessments, while an event study would still need announcement timing, market quotes and news about competing shocks (pp. 3–5, 17 and 22).

questions.question: Did the minutes change December expectations after the anticipated November hike?
questions.detail: Separate the November decision from the 10 November minutes release. Compare short-dated Swedish rates with neighbouring maturities and contemporaneous foreign moves. Jansson’s view on timing, Bunge’s emphasis on gradualism and the Governor’s six-month horizon offer distinct interpretations of an unchanged September path.

questions.question: At what level of demand did producer-cost shocks begin to reach consumers?
questions.detail: Match input prices excluding energy, pricing plans and realised consumer prices across periods of high and low utilisation. Control for the direct tax and energy effects quantified in the minutes. Hjelm’s argument predicts a changing relationship under large shocks, so a single full-sample average could conceal it.

questions.question: Was household weakness an early demand signal or a temporary survey movement?
questions.detail: Compare October confidence with subsequent durable purchases, services demand, hiring and labour utilisation as temporary fiscal support waned. The strength of retail sales before the meeting and weak consumer confidence pointed in different directions. Track which better predicted firms’ ability to maintain prices.

questions.question: How much currency pass-through remained after October’s appreciation?
questions.detail: Construct import-weighted exchange-rate changes from both February and September. Compare lagged changes with import prices net of fuel and with domestic goods inflation. Separate this channel from refining spreads and domestic demand before assigning an inflation effect to the krona’s recent rebound.
